newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ winning the war against inflation - ANZ report.
newsitem.headline: NZ winning the war against inflation - ANZ report.

text.p: Further signs of moderating activity and inflation pressures have reinforced the view that New Zealand is winning the inflation war, ANZ Investment Bank said in its Fixed Interest Monthly report released on Tuesday.
"These signs include further weakness in employment and retail sales as well as relatively subdued building sector activity even in the face of lower mortgage rates," it said.

ANZ emphasised the March quarter Household Labour Force Survey which it said pointed to a further easing in labour market pressures. Employment fell 0.1 percent over the March quarter, and the annual rate of growth eased to 1.1 percent.
ANZ said the delayed release of the Quarterly Employment Survey on June 12 would be watched closely for confirmation that a softening labour market was limiting wage pressures.
But June's key events remained the Reserve Bank's Monetary Policy Statement (MPS) on June 27 and the Government Budget the following day.
ANZ said it expected the Reserve Bank to ease its desired monetary conditions level by only 50 basis points at the June MPS -- a conservative estimated compared to some observers.

It said the RBNZ's current projections already incorporated a rapid fall in inflation over the next year and there was some doubt as to whether recent indicators suggested inflation pressures were abating much more quickly than the RBNZ expected.

"Moreover, the longer term risks to the inflation outlook arising from increased government spending will act as a constraint on the scope for the RBNZ to allow monetary conditions to ease, regardless of the potential for favourable developments over the coming year," ANZ said.
"Consequently, while we expect the RBNZ to sanction some easing in its desired monetary conditions level in the MPS, any easing is likely to be limited."

ANZ said it did not expect a slightly weaker fiscal outlook to have any impact on the government's plans to spend an additional NZ$5 billion over the next three years, because the credibility of Treasurer Winston Peters now rested on delivering the Coalition's spending promises.
A key focus for the financial markets would be details of the 1997/98 bond programme -- "an area of considerable uncertainty given New Zealand's strong fiscal position and falling net public debt".
